desc:
Walk once around the outside of a binary tree, anticlockwise, and report the values of the nodes on the boundary. The boundary is the concatenation of four parts, with no node listed twice:

  1. the root;
  2. the left boundary, top to bottom: start at the root's left child (if there is one) and keep stepping to the left child, or to the right child when there is no left child, until you reach a leaf. Every node on this walk except the leaf belongs to the left boundary. If the root has no left child the left boundary is empty;
  3. all leaves (nodes with no children), from left to right;
  4. the right boundary, bottom to top: defined like the left one but starting at the root's right child and preferring the right child over the left; the final leaf is excluded and the nodes are listed in reverse order (deepest first).

If the root itself is a leaf the answer is just [root]. The empty tree gives the empty array.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [1, -1, 2, 3, 4] the answer is [1, 3, 4, 2]: the root 1, an empty left boundary, the leaves 3 and 4, and the right boundary [2]. For tree = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] it is [1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 3].
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Split the work into three independent parts: the left edge, the leaves, and the right edge. Handle the root and the empty-tree and single-node cases separately.

For the left edge, walk down from the root's left child, preferring left children, and stop at a leaf without recording it. The right edge is the mirror image; collect it top-down and reverse it at the end.

Collect the leaves with any traversal that visits left before right (iterative preorder). Because leaves are excluded from both edges, no value is repeated. Output: root, left edge, leaves, reversed right edge.
editorial: The three parts can be computed independently. The left edge is a single downward walk that prefers left children (falling back to the right child when the left one is missing) and records every non-leaf node it meets. The right edge is the same walk with the roles of left and right swapped; because it has to be reported bottom-up, collect it in a list and reverse it. The leaves are obtained by a depth-first traversal that visits the left child first and records nodes without children.

Pay attention to the corner cases: a root that is a leaf (the answer is just that root), a root with only one child (a root with only a right child has an empty left boundary, and the right child starts the right boundary or is a leaf), and the rule that leaves never appear in an edge, which is what prevents duplicates. Everything is a single pass over the tree: O(n) time, O(n) space for the stack and output.
